🚦 RACHAKONDA POLICE – TRAFFIC ADVISORY 🚦

In view of the #TelanganaRising_Global_Summit_2025 scheduled on 8th & 9th December at Bharat Future City, special traffic arrangements will be in place.

Traffic will be regulated and diverted on all routes leading towards the summit venue to ensure smooth vehicular movement. Commuters heading in this direction are advised to plan travel in advance and use alternate routes wherever possible.

Your cooperation is appreciated in helping us ensure a safe and seamless traffic flow.

#RachakondaPolice #TrafficAdvisory #TelanganaRising2025 #BharatFutureCity

In view of the 20th Session of the Intergovernmental Committee for Intangible Cultural Heritage at Red Fort from 08–13 December 2025, special traffic arrangements will remain in force from 08:00 AM to 09:00 PM.

📍 ROADS WITH RESTRICTIONS & POSSIBLE DIVERSIONS
Netaji Subhash Marg & Nishad Raj Marg (Need-based diversions from Chhatta Rail Chowk, T-Point Subhash Marg, Shanti Van Chowk, GPO Chowk, Delhi Gate & Hanuman Mandir Crossing)
📍 PARKING
Use ONLY designated parking areas: Parade Ground | ASI Parking (Red Fort) | Dangal Maidan | Omaxe Mall | Church Mission Road Parking
📍No roadside/unauthorised parking.
📍 FOR PEDESTRIANS
Use footpaths & designated crossings. Follow on-ground staff instructions.
📍 AREAS LIKELY TO BE AFFECTED
Ring Road (Rajghat–ISBT Kashmiri Gate)| Netaji Subhash Marg | Nishad Raj Marg | SPM Marg
📍Stay updated through Delhi Traffic Police channels.

TRAFFIC ADVISORY

In view of the “AP Dhillon: One Of One Tour” at Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium (Main Arena) on 07.12.2025, special traffic arrangements will remain in force to ensure smooth movement and public convenience.

📍 ROADS TO AVOID (03:00 PM – 11:00 PM)
•IP Marg (MGM)
•Vikas Marg
•Ring Road (Rajghat → IP Depot)
Heavy vehicles will NOT be allowed on Rajghat–IP Marg stretch.
📍 DIVERSION / RESTRICTION
Need-based diversions on IP Marg / Vikas Marg as required.
📍 ENTRY TO STADIUM
* Gate 07 & 08 – Via Velodrome Road
* Gate 21, 22 & 23 – Via MGM Road
* Gate 16 & 18 – Via MGM Road
📍 PARKING
* Limited parking for labelled vehicles only
* Parking label must be displayed with vehicle number written on it
* Approach via Ring Road; parking entry from MGM Road
* Vehicles without valid labels will not be allowed near the venue
📍 GENERAL VEHICLES
No parking on Ring Road (Rajghat → IP Flyover) on event day. Violators will be towed & prosecuted.
📍Stay updated through Delhi Traffic Police channels

#DPTrafficAdvisory

data.raw_text:
Woman of the Day US Army Nurse Corps Chief First Lt Annie Fox, born in 1893 in Nova Scotia, the first woman to be awarded the Purple Heart for combat service. She was on duty when the first wave of Japanese bombers attacked Pearl Harbor at 7.55am OTD in 1941, and her immediate and sustained actions throughout the day saved lives.

Annie actually served during both World Wars. Having emigrated to the USA as a child and subsequently training as a nurse, she enlisted in the Army Nurse Corps in 1918 and served in New York during the influenza pandemic that year.

Post-WW1, there were limited opportunities for women in the ANC - even by 1941, there were only about 1,000 army nurses - but her service took her to Fort Sam Houston in Texas, Fort Mason in San Diego, and to the Philippines, where she became very skilled at tropical medicine and emergency care before pitching up in Honolulu.

Annie took over nursing supervision as Chief Nurse at the newly opened 30-bed Station Hospital at Hickam Field, adjacent to Pearl Harbor naval base, in November 1941. One month later, the Japanese attacked.

The first bombing wave fell directly on Hickam Field, destroying hangars and barracks only yards from the hospital. Annie calmly ordered all available nurses (only six were on duty) and corpsmen to their stations while explosions shook the building and machine-gun fire from low-flying aircraft rattled windows and walls. Japanese planes flew so low that pilots were visible from the hospital windows.

Within minutes, casualties poured in: airmen with severe burns, shrapnel wounds, fractured limbs, and blast injuries. Annie directed the conversion of every available space — corridors, porches, lawn — into treatment areas and carried out rapid triage of casualties. When the beds ran out, she ensured mattresses were laid on the floor.

With surgeons overwhelmed, she administered anaesthesia (ether and pentothal) for emergency operations, assisted in amputations and wound debridement, and supervised blood transfusions using limited plasma supplies.

For the whole time, Annie repeatedly exposed herself to strafing and bombing while moving between wards and the operating room to check on patients and staff. She refused to take cover when the Japanese started strafing the hospital grounds - “I’m not going to hide under a table while my boys are dying out there” — and her calm, steady voice kept panic from spreading among both staff and wounded. “We have work to do,” she said over and over. “Keep moving.”

When the second wave of bombing started and a corpsman asked if they should evacuate the building, Annie was quite clear: “No one is leaving this hospital until every man who can be saved is treated.”

She remained at her post throughout the morning and into the afternoon, only standing down when the immediate crisis eased many hours later and after she had arranged ambulance transfers for the most critical cases

Army medical records and survivor accounts confirm that Hickam Field suffered the highest Army Air Forces casualties of the day (189 killed, hundreds wounded), but the survival rate of those reaching Annie’s hospital was exceptionally high because of the rapid, organised response she directed from the first moments of the attack and the way she maintained order in the chaos.

“Rank doesn’t matter today — only how fast you can work.”

In 1943, the criteria for the Purple Heart changed: you had to be injured in the line of duty to qualify and it was made retrospective. Annie risked her life over and over but was not injured and so her Purple Heart was rescinded and replaced with the Bronze Star Medal. It seems a rather petty decision to me. It in no way detracts from her exceptional leadership and valour under fire.

Annie retired as a Major in 1945 and died in 1983, aged 93. She spoke of her award only once after the San Diego Union-Tribune tracked her down in December 1979 and refused further interviews:

“It was just another day of nursing — only louder.”
